
## Descriptive Analysis

<!-- spatial analysis -->
Visualizing trips at different spatial resolutions (community areas and H3 hexagons 6 and 7) shows how trip demand is heavily concentrated in the downtown and in the northwest at the O'Hare Airport 
(@fig-demand-by-spatial-unit-h3, @fig-demand-by-spatial-unit-ca). This makes sense due to the high concentration of offices, hotels, restaurants and other points of interest in the downtown area and 
taking into account that the O'Hare Airport is one of the busiest in the world. This same pattern can also be seen when analyzing demand through a kernel density estimation (@fig-trips-kde). Since the dataset only provides each trip's community-area centroid, we improved the KDE by scattering each area's trips uniformly at random within its polygon before smoothing. Visualizing
the KDE at different times during the day does not show any significant changes to the pattern (@fig-trips-kde-tod).
The contrast between these high-demand zones and the rest of the city is visible in all spatial resolutions. There is no noticeable 
difference when comparing demand patterns between pickup and dropoff coordinates, which is expected, since every pickup must correspond to a dropoff, so demand is symmetric across origins and destinations.

Additionally, multiple trip attributes were spatially visualized at the same spatial resolutions. Visualizing the average fare (@fig-price-by-spatial-unit-h3, @fig-price-by-spatial-unit-ca) and trip miles 
(@fig-miles-by-spatial-unit-h3, @fig-miles-by-spatial-unit-ca) per trip shows a very similar pattern, which is expected, since trip distance directly affects the price. 
They are both highest for pickups at O'Hare airport, which makes intuitive sense, since passengers flying into Chicago are typically traveling to hotels, offices, or residences spread 
across the city, resulting in long trips. The Midway airport in the southwest shows a similar but less pronounced effect. The downtown core shows consistently short pickup distances and lower prices, reflecting 
short urban trips between nearby destinations within the city center. This contrast between airport and downtown is more pronounced in the pickup maps than the dropoff maps. A very similar pattern can be observed
when visualizing trip duration (@fig-duration-by-spatial-unit-h3, @fig-duration-by-spatial-unit-ca).
Displaying the average idle time shows highest values around the two airports (@fig-idle-by-spatial-unit-h3, @fig-idle-by-spatial-unit-ca). Airport pickups are regulated through 
designated taxi holding lots where drivers must queue and wait for dispatch, artificially inflating idle time compared to city street hailing where drivers can cruise actively. The dropoff maps 
show no comparable hotspots. Drivers dropping off at the airport immediately join the holding queue, but passengers picked up at the airport are distributed across the entire 
city, so no single dropoff zone accumulates unusual idle time. Additionally, the tip rate (tips/fare) was spatially analyzed (@fig-tips-by-spatial-unit-h3, @fig-tips-by-spatial-unit-ca). The tip rate is highest for pickups at O'Hare, 
aligning with the trip distance finding. Airport passengers taking long trips tend to tip more generously, possibly because the fare is higher and tipping feels more expected 
for longer journeys. Midway airport shows a similar effect. Additionally, downtown shows an increased tip-rate. This reflects the demographic of passengers in that area, which 
include tourists, business travelers, and higher-income residents who predominantly tip more generously.

Spatially comparing the trip start times between pickup and dropoff also shows an interesting 
pattern (@fig-start-time-by-spatial-unit-h3, @fig-start-time-by-spatial-unit-ca). It shows how the airports stand out as having very late average starting hours compared to the rest of the city (ca. 17:00pm), 
while, looking at trip dropoffs, the airports stand out as having the earliest start hours. Additionally, when examining the dropoff maps, it stands out that there is a high concentration of late trips in the northern part 
of Chicago, which may be attributed to a higher concentration of destinations like restaurants.

<!-- other analysis -->
Beyond spatial patterns, the trip data was also analysed across temporal dimensions. Taxi demand follows a clear daily pattern with a morning peak of around 8-9h and an evening peak at 17h (@fig-demand-by-hour). This pattern 
reflects the start and end of the work day. At the weekly level (@fig-demand-by-day), weekdays are shown to have the highest demand with Wednesday and Thursday being the busiest days, showing that 
Chicago's taxi demand is primarily business commuter driven. Monthly (@fig-demand-by-month) demand shows how demand is lowest in winter, with peaks in May, June and October. Combining the hourly and daily views in a 
heatmap (@fig-demand-heatmap) reveals that weekend demand lacks the morning and evening peaks seen on weekdays, instead being spread more evenly across the day. 

Weather conditions also influence several trip attributes. Rain consistently increases trip demand across all hours of the day (@fig-rain-demand), as people who might 
otherwise walk or use bicycles switch to taxis in bad weather. Rain also slightly increases the tip rate (@fig-rain-tip-rate) and reduces the idle time (@fig-rain-idle-time). Here, the general pattern is also interesting with 
the tip rate being highest in the morning and idle time being at its lowest when the workday starts and ends. Visualizing the idle time distribution (@fig-idle-distribution) additionally reveals how most drivers find new passengers relatively quickly 
(< 20min). Additionally, analyzing fare per mile also shows the highest values during the morning and evening, 
which may reflect more stop-and-go traffic increasing time-based fare components relative to distance (@fig-rain-fare-per-mile). Trip distance and duration both show an interesting spike in the early morning (@fig-rain-duration, @fig-rain-distance), which can be attributed to airport 
runs. Rain has a very small effect here, slightly increasing the duration and decreasing the distance.
